title: Web Development Frameworks for More Complex Projects

intro.text: So far the pages you've directed have used plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. That works fine for small projects, but real web services — with routing, optimization, and their own servers — call for heavier machinery, and you need to know what that machinery is to judge whether your AI is using it well. This chapter introduces web development frameworks, gets Node.js installed on your machine (yes, yours — it's the environment you'll use to run and check the AI's work), and has you direct the creation of your very first Next.js app. Along the way you'll learn what localhost:3000 actually means and meet the two core Next.js ideas (components and the App Router) that let you give precise instructions and verify they were followed.

intro.title: Before you continue
intro.text: Lessons 6.2 and 6.2b cover the same skill — installing Node.js — on different operating systems. Work through the one that matches your laptop; you only need one of them.

lessons.title: Introduction to Web Development Frameworks
lessons.objective: Understand what a web development framework is — well enough to know why your AI should build on one, and to recognize the tools this course will use.

steps.title: What is a web development framework?

blocks.text: A framework literally means a skeleton or frame — a skeleton tool for web development. It bundles the features web services need over and over — so the project gets them all at once instead of the AI building each one from scratch:
Image optimization and rendering optimization
A built-in web server of its own
File-based routing (URLs that follow your folder structure)
Data caching and automatic screen updates

Think of it as a meal kit: a finished dish gets to the table quickly without prepping every ingredient from scratch. If every one of those details were implemented by hand, both the code you'd have to review and your AI token consumption would balloon — so unless a project is truly simple, developers (human or AI) build on top of a framework. “Are we on a framework?” is one of the first questions a manager should ask about any web project.

blocks.title: Workspace note
blocks.text: Your HTML/CSS/JS knowledge is still every bit as useful. Frameworks are ultimately built on top of those three, so you absolutely need the foundational concepts to judge what the AI produces.

steps.title: The framework we'll use in this course: Next.js

blocks.alt: Framework survey example from the guidebook.
blocks.caption: Framework survey example from the guidebook.

blocks.text: Next.js usage among web frameworks, 2018–2025 (source: State of JavaScript 2025).
Next.js is a widely used React framework. The chart is a survey example, not a count of all developers or companies.
It provides powerful features for building complex web services fast, which is why most companies have adopted it.

You've probably heard of React — another hugely popular library. Next.js is best thought of as an extended edition that includes React inside it, so everything React can do works exactly the same in Next.js.

steps.title: A companion tool you need to know: Node.js

blocks.text: To run a Next.js app on your own computer — which you must do to check the AI's work with your own eyes — you need Node.js.
Node.js is a program that executes JavaScript code.
If Next.js is a video game, Node.js is the game console that runs it.

lessons.title: Creating Your First Next.js App
lessons.objective: Direct the generation of your first Next.js app with npx, and read its core configuration file, package.json, well enough to audit what a project depends on.

steps.title: Generate the Next app

blocks.title: Back from the Node.js setup guide
blocks.text: Git, Node.js, and npm are ready. Now follow Steps 1 and 2 of this lesson to create and run your app. If you already created ohana-link in the GitHub guide, keep it: read the command explanations, skip the creation command, and use the existing app in Step 2.

blocks.title: Move to webdev and verify the path

blocks.text: In VS Code, choose Terminal → New Terminal. Run the commands below one at a time, outside Claude Code.
cd ~/webdev
blocks.label: Terminal command
blocks.note: Paste and press Enter. If the folder is not found, stop and check its location before continuing.

blocks.text: pwd
blocks.label: Terminal command
blocks.note: Paste into the named input area. Press Enter to run.

blocks.text: The displayed path must end in webdev. If ohana-link already contains package.json, skip the creation command and open that existing app in Step 2. If that folder exists but is incomplete, ask for help before creating another copy.

blocks.title: Your existing webdev folder is somewhere else?

blocks.text: Keep using that folder. In VS Code, choose File → Open Folder and select your existing webdev folder. Choose Terminal → New Terminal, then run pwd to confirm its location. Continue with app creation below only if ohana-link does not already exist.

blocks.title: Create ohana-link only if it does not already exist

blocks.text: npx create-next-app@latest ohana-link --use-npm
blocks.label: Terminal command
blocks.note: Paste into the named input area. Press Enter to run.

blocks.text: If asked to install create-next-app, type y and press Enter. Select Yes, use recommended defaults when that question appears. Wait for the success message and for the normal terminal prompt to return.
npx: a tool installed alongside Node.js that runs a specific command immediately.
create-next-app: the command that generates a new Next.js app.
ohana-link: the name of the app (and folder) that will be created.
“A “Next app” is not a mobile app — it means a web app built with Next.js. Feature-rich websites are usually called web applications (web apps).”
blocks.title: Another way to think about it

blocks.text: The creation command reports success and the terminal prompt returns. If you reused an existing app, its folder contains package.json.

steps.title: Run the app

blocks.text: Choose File → Open Folder in VS Code and open your existing ohana-link folder. Confirm package.json appears in Explorer. Choose Terminal → New Terminal. Run the check below in this regular terminal, outside Claude Code.
ls package.json
blocks.label: Check the app folder
blocks.note: Continue only when package.json is listed. If it is not found, open your existing ohana-link folder in VS Code, then open a new terminal.

blocks.text: npm run dev
blocks.label: Terminal command
blocks.note: Paste into the named input area. Press Enter to run.

blocks.text: Open the Local address printed in the terminal. It is usually http://localhost:3000; if Next.js chooses another port, use the printed address. Keep that terminal running. To stop the server, click the terminal and press Control + C.
ENOENT or package.json not found: the terminal is in the wrong folder. Run the app from ohana-link, where package.json is stored.
Windows says npm.ps1 cannot be loaded: use npm.cmd run dev. You do not need to change PowerShell security settings.
Cannot find module @tailwindcss/turbopack: open the Tailwind error guide in a new tab. Use it only for this exact error, then return here.
For a different error, keep the message and ask for help before reinstalling or creating another app.
The Next.js page opens in your browser without an error. Ready alone is not enough; check the browser page before continuing. Keep the server terminal running.

steps.title: Read package.json in the editor

blocks.text: In VS Code Explorer, open your app’s package.json. If Explorer shows webdev, expand ohana-link first. Read the fields below; no changes are needed.
package.json is the file a manager should read first in any Node project — it holds the project's core configuration:
name / version: the project's name and version.
scripts: a collection of frequently used commands.
dependencies: the list of tools the project depends on — the ingredients of the dish, e.g. next, react.
devDependencies: tools needed only during development — the knife and cutting board of the kitchen.
Look inside scripts for the commands available in your project. The exact entries depend on the version and options used to create it.

rows: Run the app in development mode

blocks.text: Any command registered under scripts can be run as npm run <script-name>. npm itself is the package-management program installed together with Node.js.
On Windows PowerShell, use npm.cmd in place of npm for the commands in this table.
You can locate scripts and dependencies in your project’s package.json.

steps.title: Meet the node_modules folder

blocks.text: node_modules is where the tools listed in dependencies and devDependencies actually get installed — think of it as the project's refrigerator.
It's enormous, so it's normally excluded when a project goes to GitHub or gets shared — seeing it in a repo is a sign of sloppy setup.
The dependency files describe which packages to install. When package-lock.json exists, npm ci restores its recorded versions. npm install installs the dependencies and can update the lockfile.

blocks.title: Only if an existing app is missing its packages

blocks.text: A newly created app already has its packages; skip this section. If you are restoring an existing app, stop its development server with Control+C first. Keep package.json and package-lock.json. Use a regular terminal in the folder containing package.json and run only one of the following commands.
npm ci
blocks.label: Terminal command

blocks.text: npm install
blocks.label: Terminal command
blocks.note: Use this when there is no package-lock.json.

blocks.text: Wait for the command to finish successfully before starting the server again. Keep the lockfile when sharing the project so others can restore the same recorded package versions.

lessons.title: How a Next.js App Runs
lessons.objective: Get to the heart of how npm run dev makes an app reachable at http://localhost:3000 — well enough to confirm for yourself that a server the AI claims is “running” really is.

steps.title: A Next app has its own built-in server

blocks.title: Reuse your running server
blocks.text: If the app from Lesson 6.4 is still running, keep that terminal open and read the output below. Do not start a second server. Use this command in the ohana-link folder only when the server is stopped.

blocks.title: Start the server only if it is stopped

blocks.text: npm run dev
blocks.label: Terminal command
blocks.note: Paste into the named input area. Press Enter to run.

blocks.text:
> ohana-link@0.1.0 dev
▲ Next.js 16.2.0 (Turbopack)
- Local:    http://localhost:3000
- Network:  http://172.30.1.87:3000
✓ Ready in 412ms
blocks.label: Example output — do not type

blocks.text: Running npm run dev starts Next.js's own embedded web server.
When your browser visits that address, the server responds with HTML/CSS/JS files, and the browser draws the screen.
When the AI reports “the server is running,” this output — especially the ✓ Ready line and the Local: address — is the evidence to look for.
The terminal shows Ready and a Local address, and that address opens your app in the browser without an error. Keep this terminal open.

steps.title: What is localhost?

blocks.text: localhost is the address that points to your own computer.
So visiting http://localhost:3000 means sending a request to the Next server running on your own machine.
Nobody else can reach your server through their localhost — to each person, localhost means themselves. Keep this in mind before flagging “the link doesn't work for me” as a bug.

steps.title: The role of the port number

blocks.text: The :3000 after localhost is a port number.
Several servers can run on one computer at the same time, so there has to be a way to tell which server a request is meant for.
A port number is like a gate number — the operating system assigns each server its own unique one.

steps.title: Why don't normal websites show a port number?

blocks.text: Everyday websites — Google, YouTube — connect with just the address, no port in sight.
That's because the browser automatically uses port 443, the HTTPS default.
It's a globally agreed-upon default, so there's simply no need to display it.

steps.title: Recap

rows: The address that points to my own computer
The port number used during development (Next.js's default)
The web's standard HTTPS port — the invisible default every browser assumes

blocks.text: Public HTTPS addresses usually omit port 443. A hosting platform can forward requests to an application running on another internal port.

lessons.title: Next.js Core Concepts
lessons.objective: Nail down the first concepts you need when directing Next.js work: component-based development, and page routing with the App Router — the vocabulary for scoping AI edits and checking where files landed.

steps.title: Core concept: pages are assembled from pieces

blocks.text: Instead of drawing a whole page in one go, Next.js splits the UI into small pieces, builds each separately, and assembles them like Lego blocks into a finished page.
Each individual UI piece is called a component — for example a Header, a Sidebar, or a Timer.
A page itself is just another component — a page component assembled from many smaller ones.
Why split things up?
Built as a single HTML/CSS/JS file, all the UI code piles into one place and grows steadily more complex.
When it's hard for humans and AI to read, both maintenance and generation quality suffer.
Splitting by component separates responsibilities, making editing and reuse much easier — and making the AI's changes far easier to review.

In VS Code Explorer, right-click the ohana-link folder and choose New File. Type prompt.md and press Enter. The new file should appear directly inside ohana-link, alongside package.json. Paste the prompt below into this file. Save with Ctrl + S on Windows or Command + S on Mac. Next, create and save settings.json in the following step.

Build a Pomodoro timer web application.

# Main Page

## Main Page UI
- Display the title "pomodoro" using an `h1` tag
- Display the current remaining time (load and use from localStorage, default is 25 minutes)
- Place Start, Stop, and Reset buttons
- Place a Settings button (navigates to the Settings page)

## Main Page Features
- Clicking the Start button starts the timer
- Clicking the Stop button pauses/stops the timer
- Clicking the Reset button resets the timer

# Settings Page

## Settings Page UI
- Place the title "Setting" using an `h3` tag
- Place a single input field to set the timer duration
- Place a Complete Setting (Save) button

## Settings Page Features
- Change timer duration
- Can only be set between 1 minute and 60 minutes (inclusive)
- The Complete Setting button cannot be clicked if the input field is left empty
- The updated time is immediately reflected on the Main Page
- The updated time persists even after a page refresh

# Component Splitting
- Properly split the work into modular components
- Split the components into `Timer`, `Controllers`, and `TimerSettingInput`
- Store the components in the `/components` folder
- If a `src` folder exists, store them in `src/components`
- Must be stored in `/components`, NOT `app/components`

# Miscellaneous
- Do not build or run the Next.js app after completing the development
- Explain the results in English as follows:
- Explain unit by unit for each component (Name, Path, Role)
- Explain in the order of Regular Components -> Page Components
- In the Page Component explanation, include a list of the Regular Components it contains

steps.title: A look inside a component file

blocks.text: Find Timer.tsx in Explorer and open it. Read the interface and behavior together; no edit is required.
Open the generated Timer.tsx and you'll find two things living together in one file:
HTML tags — the element's appearance and layout.
JavaScript functions — the element's behavior.
A .tsx file contains TypeScript with JSX, which looks similar to HTML. Components can combine the interface and the logic that supports it.
You can identify the interface markup and the logic in the component file.

steps.title: App Router: the folder structure IS the URL

blocks.text: Unlike ordinary components, page components are saved under the app/ folder with the file name page.tsx — and the URL follows the folder path exactly. That mapping is your audit trail: given a URL, you know exactly which file to inspect.

The test page file exists under app/test or src/app/test, and the running app opens at /test.

steps.title: Concept summary

rows: One reusable UI piece bundling appearance (HTML) and behavior (JS)
A component saved as page.tsx under app/ — it becomes a page
Next.js routing where the app/ folder structure maps directly to URLs
File format that holds TypeScript (JavaScript) and HTML together
